extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of philosophy of science, logic, and the foundations of mathematics
extracted.subtask_description: Principles and standards for judging mathematical/geometrical reasoning and for assessing evidence, belief, and disbelief in scientific claims (including how to treat purported miracles and laws). Focuses on what constitutes sufficient evidence, when to reject claims or laws, and the axiomatic premises of number and geometry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Connotation of number names
rubrics_metrics.description: The name of a number connotes a physical property of an aggregate (the characteristic manner in which the agglomeration is made up of, and may be separated into, parts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: calling a collection 'three' implies it can be formed by one+one+one or by adding one pebble to an aggregate called 'two'. The explanation emphasizes physical distinguishability (two apples vs three) and uses concrete modes of formation (pebbles) to ground numerical meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select a uniform mode of formation for numerical nomenclature
rubrics_metrics.description: For convenience and simplicity, fix the connotation of number names on one uniform principle or mode of formation for each number.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advantages: simplicity aids understanding and retention. Our numeral system conveys two modes of formation (successive unit addition via place in the series, and decomposition into units and powers of ten via the spoken name and numeral). Choosing a consistent mode helps derive other modes deductively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arithmetic grounded on the inductive law 'the sums of equals are equals'
rubrics_metrics.description: Arithmetic rests on an inductive generalization: 'The sums of equals are equals' (and related axioms), which serves as the warrant for arithmetic calculations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operations and propositions in arithmetic are applications of this comprehensive law; elementary demonstrations proceed from such inductive truths combined with number definitions (example: deriving 5 + 2 = 7 by unit addition).

rubrics_metrics.name: Algebraic notation as requisite for general reasoning about functions
rubrics_metrics.description: Algebraic notation is required to express general relations between numbers and functions so that propositions about all numbers (not particular numbers) can be stated and manipulated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Algebra frames the general problem: given F as a function of a number, find what function F will be of any function of that number. Examples: binomial theorem (expressing (a + b)^n in terms of a, b, n) and viewing equation resolution as determining what function a variable is of other quantities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resolution of equations as general functional propositions
rubrics_metrics.description: Solving an equation is a general theorem answering: if b is a function of x (and other parameters), what function is x of b and the parameters?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: solving x^2 + ax = b gives x as a specific function of a and b; resolution of equations fits the general algebraic problem of functions of functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geometry's fundamental axioms and definitional premises
rubrics_metrics.description: Geometry presumes a few general laws/axioms (e.g., sums of equals are equal; things equal to the same thing are equal to one another; magnitudes that can be made to coincide are equal) together with definitions that assert the real existence of objects (straight lines, circles, angles, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These premises are regarded as ultimate premises of geometry, enabling deduction of many derivative truths. The text argues these axioms are empirical general laws of nature, not mere verbal definitions, and gives examples (straight lines diverging, equality of radii).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduce positional/qualitative questions to quantitative measurement when possible
rubrics_metrics.description: Questions of position and figure can be resolved into questions of magnitude via coordinate-like reduction (positions determined by rectangular coordinates), thus converting qualitative spatial problems into quantitative measurements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This reduction explains why geometry is highly deductive: general axioms about equality propagate to many consequences, and a few measured quantities (lines, angles) can determine many others (as in trigonometric survey methods).

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on applicability of mathematical methods to other sciences
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical principles apply advantageously only when numerical laws of causes can be ascertained by proper induction and when causes are not so numerous/complex/fluctuating as to make computation infeasible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mathematics is unsuitable where causes are hidden or numerous (e.g., complex chemistry, physiology, social phenomena). Mathematical accuracy often comes 'at the expense of the reality of the inquiry' beyond astronomy-like domains; the method is valuable chiefly as methodological training for deductive reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between mere absence of belief and active disbelief
rubrics_metrics.description: Disbelief is not merely lacking belief; it is the mental state in which one is fully persuaded that some opinion is false, such that even strong apparent evidence would be judged false or mistaken.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The chapter emphasizes that grounds for abstaining from belief (insufficient proof) differ from grounds for positive disbelief (evidence against the proposition).

rubrics_metrics.name: Improbability vs impossibility: comparison of approximate vs complete inductions
rubrics_metrics.description: If an allegation contradicts approximate generalizations on both sides, decide by comparing probabilities (improbability). If it contradicts a completed generalization (a law grounded on rigorous induction), it is impossible and must be disbelieved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Hume's doctrine reinterpreted—assertions contradictory to a complete induction are incredible; but where only approximate generalizations exist, weigh the relative strength of inductions to decide. The text explains that 'impossibility' is reserved for contradiction to a full, well-established induction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hierarchy of evidence: laws from experimentum crucis outrank testimonial/perceptual evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: A law established by critical experiments (experimentum crucis) and repeated tests (excluding observer error) has such strength that any alleged single occurrence contradicting it (without counteracting cause) should be disbelieved unless evidence overturning the law is equivalent in strength.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an antecedent A has been repeatedly shown to produce effect B, then an assertion that A occurred without B (and no counteracting cause) must be rejected unless evidence comparable to that which established the law is produced. Testimonial or perceptual claims are only approximate generalizations and are weaker.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard for overturning an established law
rubrics_metrics.description: To reject a law of nature, the new evidence must be of equivalent strength to the evidence by which the law was established (i.e., sufficient to show a flaw in the original induction).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If evidence against a law is more plausibly explained by error in the experiments/interpretation that established the law, one should retain the law; only truly equivalent contrary evidence should compel abandoning it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to identify counteracting causes when alleging contradiction to causal laws
rubrics_metrics.description: An alleged case of a known cause A existing without its usual effect B must show that no adequate counteracting cause was present to explain the absence of B; otherwise it is not a true contradiction of the causal law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text notes that mere non-occurrence of an effect when its cause is present is common if counteracting conditions exist; only absence of any adequate counteracting cause would make the anomaly significant against the law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of miracles as hypotheses invoking new causes
rubrics_metrics.description: A miracle is not a contradiction to the law of causation but is alleged to be produced by a new cause (a supernatural intervention); acceptance of such an account depends on the prior plausibility of a being capable of such intervention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if the extraordinary event is well attested, one cannot prove it is a miracle (i.e., supernatural) because the alternative of an unknown natural cause cannot be entirely excluded. Those who already believe in supernatural agents have to weigh which hypothesis (supernatural vs unknown natural) is more probable given the character attributed to the agent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Completeness of induction determined by scientific canons
rubrics_metrics.description: We are justified in declaring an induction 'complete' (and thereby treating contradiction to it as impossible) only when the scientific canons of induction indicate that completeness is achievable in the case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: in cases with experimentum crucis and exhaustive testing by many observers such that error is excluded, we may treat the induction as complete; otherwise we must remain open to revision.
